The Columbia is the largest river of the Pacific Northwest of North America. It rises in the Rocky Mountains of British Columbia, flows south into Washington State, then turns west to form most of the border with Oregon before it meets the Pacific. It runs about 2,000 kilometres, and its biggest tributary is the Snake.

For thousands of years it was a river of salmon. Each year the fish ran upriver to spawn, and the peoples along its banks built their lives around the runs:

  • Near the mouth lived Chinookan peoples such as the Chinook, Clatsop and Kathlamet.
  • Upriver, at the great falls and rapids, lived the Wasco and Wishram, and on the plateau the Yakama, Umatilla and others. See Plateau fishers and hunter-gatherers.
  • Further north, Interior Salish peoples such as the Colville and Okanagan fished at Kettle Falls.

Places like Celilo Falls and Kettle Falls drew people from far away each summer, and became markets where dried fish, shells, furs and later horses changed hands. The Chinook trade language grew out of this traffic.

An American captain, Robert Gray, sailed into the river in 1792 and named it after his ship. The Lewis and Clark expedition reached its mouth in 1805, and the Hudson's Bay Company ran the fur trade of the region from forts on its banks. In the 1900s big dams such as the Grand Coulee made power and watered farms, but they blocked the salmon and drowned Celilo Falls in 1957.
